notes.meaning: Two members of the priestly tribe of Levi, later named as Amram and Jochebed, marry and start a family. They already had two older children, Miriam and Aaron, before the king's cruel law was issued. God was quietly preparing a godly household to bring forth both Israel's deliverer and its priestly line.

Jochebed gives birth to a healthy baby boy and sees that he is unusually lovely and special in God's sight. She hides him in her home for three months to protect him from Pharaoh's deadly command. Her brave choice was driven by trust in God rather than fear of the king.

When the baby can no longer be hidden safely at home, his mother weaves a small chest out of sturdy papyrus reeds. She coats it with tar and pitch to keep it waterproof, places the child inside, and rests it among the tall reeds along the Nile River. Instead of giving in to despair, she entrusts her child's life to God's care.

The baby's older sister, Miriam, waits at a safe distance to watch what will happen to her brother. Her watchful care shows the family's lingering hope even in a desperate hour. God used her presence to guide the next steps of the child's rescue.

Pharaoh's daughter comes down to bathe in the Nile while her royal attendants walk along the riverbank. She notices the basket hidden among the reeds and sends her servant girl to bring it to her. God arranged the timing so that the child would be found by the king's own daughter.

The princess opens the basket and finds the baby boy crying. Her heart fills with pity, and she realizes right away that he is one of the Hebrew children. God used the baby's tears to soften the heart of a royal Egyptian woman.

Miriam steps forward and asks the princess if she should find a Hebrew woman to nurse the child. The princess tells her to go, so the girl runs and brings the baby's own mother. God used Miriam's quick courage to reunite the baby with his mother.

Pharaoh's daughter tells the mother to take the child home, nurse him, and receive wages for her work. The mother takes her son back into her arms, now protected by royal authority. God not only spared the child's life, but also rewarded the mother's faith with peace and provision.

After the child grows older and is weaned, his mother brings him back to the palace, where the princess adopts him. She names him Moses, which sounds like the word for drawing out, because she drew him from the river. In the palace, Moses received a royal education that God would later turn toward His own good purposes.

Moses grows to full manhood and goes out to observe the harsh labor of his Hebrew brothers firsthand. While there, he sees an Egyptian beating one of his fellow Israelites. His heart is moved with grief and loyalty for his oppressed people, choosing to stand with them rather than enjoy royal ease.

Moses looks around to ensure no one is watching, strikes down the Egyptian oppressor, and buries the body in the sand. He acted out of a deep desire to deliver his people, knowing God had called him to rescue them. Still, his need to look around showed that his faith was mixed with human fear.

differ.view: Moses acted in hasty self-reliance and the energy of the flesh, attempting to accomplish God's deliverance through unlawful violence before God's appointed time.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Moses' killing of the Egyptian shows human presumption and an unauthorized use of force rather than divine guidance.

notes.meaning: Moses returns the next day and finds two Hebrews fighting each other. He steps in as a peacemaker and asks the man in the wrong why he is striking his fellow countryman. It was painful to see God's people harming each other while already suffering under heavy slavery.

The guilty man angrily asks who made Moses a ruler and judge, and asks if Moses plans to kill him just as he killed the Egyptian. Moses realizes his secret is out and becomes terrified. The people were not yet ready to welcome his leadership, and his hopes of helping them were temporarily crushed.

Pharaoh hears about the killing and tries to put Moses to death. Moses runs away to the distant desert land of Midian, where he stops to rest beside a well. God used this exile to humble Moses and prepare him through years of quiet desert life.

The seven daughters of the priest of Midian come to draw water and fill the troughs for their father's flock. Rough local shepherds try to chase them away, but Moses steps up, protects the women, and waters their sheep. Even as a tired stranger, Moses was quick to defend the weak and do good.

When the young women return home early, their father Reuel asks why they are back so soon. They explain that an Egyptian stranger rescued them from the shepherds and even drew water for their animals. Reuel urges them to bring the man to their home so he can eat and rest.

Moses agrees to stay with Reuel, who gives his daughter Zipporah to Moses in marriage. The former prince of Egypt now lives simply as a shepherd in a foreign land. God used this humble work to teach Moses patience and shepherd-like care for others.

Zipporah gives birth to a son, and Moses names him Gershom, which means a stranger there. Moses gave him this name because he felt like an alien living far away from his family and the promised land. Even in a peaceful new home, Moses remembered that his true calling lay elsewhere.

After many years, the king of Egypt dies, but the new king keeps the Israelites under the same brutal slavery. Broken by their hard labor, the people groan and cry out for help, and their prayers rise up to heaven. Suffering finally drove them to seek God with all their hearts.

God hears the groaning of the Israelites and remembers His covenant—His binding promise—with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Remembering does not mean God had forgotten, but that the time had come for Him to act. God looked upon His suffering people with deep love, ready to set their rescue in motion.
